title: SHE WAS USED, MISTREATED, AND LEFT IN THE WILDERNESS… BUT GOD CALLED HER BY NAME.
paragraphs: SHE WAS USED, MISTREATED, AND LEFT IN THE WILDERNESS… BUT GOD CALLED HER BY NAME.
The heartbreaking story of Hagar reveals a God who sees the tears nobody notices, hears the cries nobody answers, and meets the forgotten in places where everyone else has abandoned them.
What if the place where you felt most abandoned becomes the very place where you discover that God has never taken His eyes off you?
There is a kind of pain that doesn't come from losing someone.
It comes from realizing that someone you trusted never truly valued you.
You were useful when they needed you. Important when you could give them something. Welcome when your presence served their purposes.
But when you became inconvenient…
Everything changed.
Suddenly, the people who once needed you began treating you like a burden.
Your sacrifices were forgotten. Your loyalty meant nothing. Your tears became an irritation.
And somewhere between trying to remain strong and wondering what you did wrong, a terrible question began forming inside your heart.
Does anybody actually see what I'm going through?
Not the smile you wear in public.
Not the carefully arranged photographs.
Not the familiar answer, "I'm okay," when someone asks how you're doing.
But the real you.
The exhausted you.
The wounded you.
The person who sometimes cries after everyone else has fallen asleep.
The person who keeps praying even though heaven seems painfully quiet.
The person who has been holding everything together while quietly falling apart.
If you've ever felt that way, there is a woman in Scripture you need to meet.
Her name was Hagar.
And before her story was over, she would give us one of the most intimate descriptions of God recorded in the Old Testament.
El Roi.
The God who sees me.
But what makes her story so extraordinary is not simply that God saw her.
It's where He found her.
And what He said when He did.
Hagar was an Egyptian servant in the household of Abram and Sarai, whose names God would later change to Abraham and Sarah.
She was not the woman to whom God had originally given the promise of a son.
She was not the central figure in the covenant narrative.
She was a foreigner, a servant, and a woman living within a household where other people held tremendous power over her future.
Genesis 16 introduces her almost casually.
But there was nothing casual about what happened next.
God had promised Abram descendants. Yet Sarai remained unable to bear children, and the years were passing.
Waiting had become painful.
Hope had become difficult.
And Sarai decided to take matters into her own hands.
She gave Hagar to Abram as a wife so that she might obtain children through her.
Read that slowly.
Hagar's body became part of someone else's attempt to solve a problem.
Scripture does not record Hagar being asked whether she wanted this arrangement.
We should not pretend to know every thought she had. But we must not overlook the enormous imbalance of power surrounding her.
She was a servant.
They were her masters.
And decisions that would alter the course of her life were being made above her.
Sometimes the deepest wounds begin when someone with power forgets that the person beneath them is still a human being.
Hagar conceived.
And immediately, the household began to fracture.
Genesis 16:4 tells us that after Hagar became pregnant, her mistress became despised in her eyes.
The Bible does not present Hagar as morally flawless. Her attitude toward Sarai contributed to the conflict.
But neither does it excuse what happened to her afterward.
Sarai blamed Abram.
Abram placed Hagar back under Sarai's authority.
And then Scripture records a devastating sentence.
"So Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her."
— Genesis 16:6, ESV
The Hebrew word translated "dealt harshly" comes from the verb עָנָה (ʿanah), which can describe afflicting, humbling, or oppressing someone, depending on its context.
The text does not give us every detail of Sarai's treatment.
But it gives us enough to know that Hagar was suffering.
Enough that she ran.
Pregnant.
Vulnerable.
Away from the only household in which she had been living.
Toward the wilderness.
Can you imagine that journey?
No comfortable bed waiting at the end of the road.
No guarantee of food.
No certainty about where she would deliver her child.
And perhaps the most crushing thought of all…
The people who should have protected her had become the people she was trying to escape.
Some of you understand that kind of heartbreak.
Not because your circumstances are identical to Hagar's, but because you know what it feels like to be wounded by someone you expected to care for you.
A parent whose words still echo years later.
A spouse whose betrayal changed the way you trust.
A church community where you expected compassion but encountered humiliation.
A friend who disappeared when your life became complicated.
A family that remembers your mistakes more readily than your sacrifices.
And when you finally reached the point where you couldn't take another step, you wondered whether God had noticed any of it.
Hagar was somewhere in the wilderness when the story took a turn she could never have anticipated.
God came looking for her.
Genesis 16:7 says:
"The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, the spring on the way to Shur."
That word matters.
Found.
Hagar had fled from human cruelty.
But she had not escaped divine attention.
She was outside the household.
Outside the protection she needed.
Outside the plans other people had made for her.
But she was not outside the reach of God.
And then came a question.
"Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?"
— Genesis 16:8, ESV
Notice something beautiful.
He called her Hagar.
By name.
In the previous events, she had been treated as someone whose life could be arranged around the desires of others.
But here, in the wilderness, she was personally addressed.
The God of Abraham knew the name of the Egyptian servant.
He knew where she had come from.
He knew what had happened.
And He invited her to speak.
Her answer was painfully simple.
"I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai."
She did not pretend everything was fine.
She did not disguise the situation with religious language.
She told the truth.
And the God who met her in the wilderness did not need her to manufacture a stronger version of herself before speaking to her.
Perhaps that is something you need to hear today.
You do not have to pretend your marriage is healthy when it is breaking your heart.
You do not have to call betrayal a blessing.
You do not have to deny grief to demonstrate faith.
You do not have to hide your exhaustion behind a Bible verse.
The Lord already knows.
And because He knows, you can come to Him truthfully.
But Hagar's story contains a difficult detail that responsible Bible readers must not ignore.
The angel of the LORD instructed her to return to Sarai and submit to her authority.
That command can be deeply troubling, especially to someone who has experienced abuse.
We must handle it carefully.
Genesis 16 is not a blanket command for abused people to return to dangerous situations.

It records a particular divine instruction given to Hagar within a specific historical narrative. It does not authorize mistreatment, remove accountability from oppressors, or require victims to remain in danger.
Scripture repeatedly condemns oppression and calls God's people to protect the vulnerable.
If you are being abused, seeking safety, protection, and trustworthy help is not a failure of faith.
And notice that God's message to Hagar did not end with the instruction to return.
He also gave her a promise.
Her descendants would become too numerous to count.
And He told her something about the son growing within her.
"Behold, you are pregnant and shall bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because the LORD has listened to your affliction."
— Genesis 16:11, ESV
Ishmael.
In Hebrew, יִשְׁמָעֵאל (Yishmaʿel) means "God hears" or "God has heard."
Imagine that.
Before the child was born, God gave his mother a name that would continually remind her that her suffering had not gone unnoticed.
Every time she called her son…
Ishmael.
Every time she heard someone speak his name…
Ishmael.
She would be reminded of the God who heard her affliction.
And then Hagar did something remarkable.
She spoke a name for the LORD who had spoken to her.
Genesis 16:13 records the Hebrew expression:
אֵל רֳאִי
El Ro'i.
Often rendered:
"You are a God of seeing."
Or, in the familiar devotional expression:
"The God who sees me."
The Hebrew wording is compact and has generated some discussion about its precise nuance. But its central testimony is unmistakable.
Hagar had encountered the God who saw her in her distress.
And that changed the wilderness.
Not because the wilderness suddenly became a palace.
Not because every painful circumstance immediately disappeared.
But because she discovered that she was not invisible to the LORD.
Think about the astonishing reversal.
The woman who had been treated as an instrument in someone else's plan became the woman who testified personally about the God who saw her.
The servant who had fled into the wilderness became a witness to divine compassion.
And the place that looked like the end of her story became the setting of an encounter remembered for generations.
People may overlook you without God ever losing sight of you.
But the story doesn't end there.
And this is where Hagar's experience becomes even more heartbreaking.
Years passed.
Ishmael was born.
God fulfilled His promise to Sarah, and Isaac entered the household.
Then another conflict erupted.
Genesis 21 tells us that Sarah saw Ishmael laughing, in a context that led her to demand that Hagar and her son be sent away.
The apostle Paul later describes Ishmael's conduct toward Isaac as persecution in Galatians 4:29.
The biblical account does not invite us to erase that conflict.
But neither does it erase Hagar's humanity.
Abraham was distressed because Ishmael was his son.
God assured Abraham that He would also make a nation of Ishmael, while confirming that the covenant line would continue through Isaac.
Then Abraham gave Hagar bread and water and sent her away.
And once again…
Hagar entered the wilderness.
Only this time, she was not alone.
Her son was with her.
The water eventually ran out.
There was no visible solution.
No reserve supply.
No promise from another human being that help was on its way.
And the mother who had once fled while carrying her unborn child now faced the possibility of watching that child die.
Genesis 21:16 records her anguish:
"Let me not look on the death of the child."
She sat at a distance.
And she wept.
Try to imagine the unbearable helplessness of that moment.
A mother who could not provide what her child desperately needed.
A mother whose love was greater than her resources.
A mother who could not bear to watch the suffering unfolding before her.
There are parents reading this who know something of that terror.
You have stared at medical bills you could not afford.
You have worried about how to feed your children.
You have sat beside a hospital bed, pleading with God for one more chance.
You have smiled in front of your family while privately wondering how much longer you could keep going.
You have prayed prayers so desperate that they barely sounded like words.
And perhaps you have asked the question Hagar's circumstances seem to raise.
Lord, You saw me before. Do You still see me now?
Then Scripture says something extraordinary.
"And God heard the voice of the boy."
— Genesis 21:17, ESV
There it is again.
The meaning of Ishmael's name.
God hears.
Years earlier, God had said He heard Hagar's affliction.
Now, in the wilderness, God heard her son.
The promise had not vanished simply because the circumstances had become terrifying.
And the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven.
"What troubles you, Hagar? Fear not, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is."
— Genesis 21:17, ESV
Where he is.
Not where someone thought he should be.
Not where his family wished he were.
Not where his circumstances might have been easier.
Where he is.
And then came the command to lift up the boy and hold him, accompanied by God's renewed promise to make him a great nation.
Genesis 21:19 says:
"Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water."
Read that again.
God opened her eyes.
And she saw a well.
The text does not explicitly tell us whether the well had already been there or whether God had newly provided it.
What it does tell us is that God enabled Hagar to see the provision she needed.
And she gave her son water.
The child lived.
God was with the boy as he grew.
The wilderness had not defeated the promise of God.
Now, be careful not to turn that moment into a guarantee Scripture never makes.
It does not mean every desperate situation will end exactly as we want.
It does not mean every illness will be healed immediately.
It does not mean every financial crisis will disappear overnight.
It does not mean the suffering of God's people is imaginary.
The Bible is far too honest about grief, persecution, and loss to permit those conclusions.
But Hagar's story does reveal something enduring about the character of God.
He is not indifferent to the afflicted.
He is not unaware of those pushed to the margins.
He is not limited by the failure of human beings to show compassion.
And He is faithful to His promises.
There is another truth here that we must not miss.
God's compassion toward Hagar did not mean that Ishmael replaced Isaac as the child of the covenant promise.
Genesis is clear that God's covenant with Abraham would be established through Isaac.
Yet God also promised to bless Ishmael, multiply his descendants, and remain with him.
The distinction matters.
God's covenant purposes and His compassion toward the vulnerable are not enemies.
His faithfulness to His redemptive plan did not require Him to ignore Hagar's suffering.
And that brings us to Jesus Christ.
Because Hagar's story is not simply an ancient account of a woman who survived the wilderness.
It reveals something about the God whose saving purposes unfold throughout Scripture and find their fulfillment in Christ.
We should not claim that every detail of Hagar's experience is a direct prediction of Jesus.
Nor should we pretend that Hagar and Sarah are interchangeable figures in the biblical story.
In Galatians 4:21–31, Paul uses Hagar and Sarah in an allegorical argument about slavery, freedom, law, and promise.
That passage has its own theological purpose, and it must be respected.
But when we read the whole Bible, we discover that the God who saw Hagar is the same God whose mercy is revealed decisively in His Son.
And look at the people Jesus noticed.
A woman suffering from bleeding for twelve years, whose desperate touch did not escape His attention.
A Samaritan woman at a well, whose complicated history did not prevent Him from speaking to her about living water.
A blind beggar crying out while others tried to silence him.
A tax collector despised by his community.
A thief dying beside Him.
A grieving mother walking behind the body of her only son.
Jesus did not merely notice the impressive, the powerful, or the religiously respectable.
He stopped for people others hurried past.
He spoke to people others avoided.
He welcomed repentant sinners whom self-righteous observers preferred to condemn.
And He did something infinitely greater than simply acknowledging human pain.
He came to save sinners.
Matthew 1:21 says of Jesus:
"You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins."
The Greek name Ἰησοῦς (Iēsous) corresponds to the Hebrew name Yeshua, associated with the meaning "the LORD saves."
And that is the heart of the Gospel.
The God who sees our suffering also sees our sin.
He sees the wounds inflicted upon us.
And He sees the wrongs we ourselves have committed.
He knows when we have been betrayed.
And He knows when we have betrayed others.
He knows the injustice we have endured.
And He knows the selfishness, pride, bitterness, dishonesty, and disobedience we would rather conceal.
Nothing is hidden from Him.
Yet the astonishing news of Christianity is that God did not leave humanity without hope.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, entered our broken world.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He loved the unlovely.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He welcomed the repentant.
He bore our sins on the cross.
And He rose bodily from the dead.
His resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
We are not saved because our suffering makes us righteous.
We are not forgiven because we have endured enough hardship.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
As Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches, salvation is God's gift, not something we earn through our works.
And this is where Hagar's story becomes personally searching.
Perhaps you came here because you feel forgotten.
But what if the God who sees you is also calling you to stop hiding from Him?
Not merely to ask Him to change your circumstances.
But to surrender your life.
To confess what you have been protecting.
To repent of what has been destroying you.
To release the bitterness you have been feeding.
To trust Christ with the parts of your story you have never allowed anyone else to touch.
Because the deepest hope of the Gospel is not simply that Jesus will make every difficult chapter comfortable.
It is that Jesus can redeem sinners, reconcile them to God, and begin transforming lives that once seemed beyond restoration.
He does not excuse sin.
He forgives repentant sinners.
He does not call evil good.
He overcomes evil with His goodness.
He does not promise that following Him means never entering another wilderness.
He promises His people something far more enduring.
His presence.
His grace.
His faithfulness.
And ultimately, resurrection life in a world where death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message is more than a beautiful phrase.
Not because the past never happened.
Not because every consequence disappears.
Not because the scars are always removed.
But because the grace of Jesus Christ can give a redeemed future to people whose past seemed to have written their ending.
Hagar's story was not erased.
It was remembered in Scripture.
Her tears were not meaningless.
Her son was not forgotten.
Her wilderness was not beyond God's reach.
And neither is yours.
Maybe you have spent years believing that because someone abandoned you, you must be unworthy of love.
Maybe you have confused another person's cruelty with God's opinion of you.
Maybe you have carried shame for choices you made while desperately trying to survive.
Maybe you have wandered so far spiritually that returning to prayer feels almost impossible.
Or maybe you are the person who appears spiritually strong while secretly running on empty.
You still attend church.
You still share Scripture.
You still encourage other people.
But when the room becomes quiet, you wonder whether God remembers you.
Hear this carefully.
Your pain is not proof that God has forgotten you.
And His awareness of your suffering is not permission to remain in sin.
The same Lord who invites the weary to come to Him also calls sinners to repentance and faith.
His grace is not a hiding place for rebellion.
It is the undeserved mercy that brings us home.
So bring Him the truth.
Not the polished testimony.
Not the religious performance.
Not the version of your life that looks acceptable to everyone else.
Bring Him the grief.
The fear.
The anger.
The regret.
The questions.
The sins you need to confess.
The burdens you can no longer carry.
And if you do not know how to begin, perhaps your prayer can be as simple as this:

"Lord Jesus, You know where I am. You see what has happened to me, and You see what is happening inside me. Forgive my sins. Heal what is broken according to Your wisdom. Teach me to trust Your Word instead of my fear. Give me courage to obey You, wisdom to seek help where I need it, and faith to keep walking when I cannot see the road ahead. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me, Lord. I surrender my life to You. Amen."
And if these words reached a place in your heart that you have been afraid to expose, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not have to share details you are not ready to make public.
But your words may remind someone else reading the comments that they are not the only person walking through a wilderness.
And if you have experienced God's faithfulness in a season of rejection, grief, or spiritual exhaustion, consider sharing a small part of your testimony.
Someone may be praying for the courage to believe that God has not abandoned them.
Your testimony may help them keep going.
The friend who stopped attending church.
The single mother quietly carrying too much.
The father trying to hold his family together.
The young believer struggling with shame.
The person who has become distant from God because suffering has made faith difficult.
The one who always says, "I'm fine."
Not simply to increase its reach, but because you may never know which person in your circle is silently asking whether God still sees them.
Because a life nourished by God's Word needs more than a moment of emotional inspiration.
It needs roots.
It needs truth.
It needs a growing relationship with Jesus Christ.
And that is also why I want to extend a personal invitation to those who believe in the mission of Gospel Warrior.
Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that believers may share generously in good works (2 Corinthians 9:6–8).
But we must also honor the freedom Scripture gives.
God loves a cheerful giver, not one pressured into giving.
And the Gospel itself can never be bought.
These are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
They are simply ways to express gratitude to those helping sustain the mission.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible.
We want people to open Scripture.
We want weary believers strengthened, wandering hearts called back to Christ, and new disciples equipped to grow in truth.
You can still help.
Pray for this ministry.
Pass along the free discipleship resources.
Encourage a friend to read the Bible.
Speak the name of Jesus with love and courage.
The value of your faith is not measured by your ability to make a monthly payment.
Christ is the Savior. The ministry is only a servant.
And everything we do must remain under that truth.
Now, before you leave, return with me to that woman in the wilderness.
Hagar.
The Egyptian servant.
The mistreated woman.
The mother afraid for her child.
The person who had every reason to believe she had been discarded.
Picture her near that spring in Genesis 16.
Dust on her feet.
An uncertain future ahead.
Painful memories behind.
And the voice of the LORD calling her by name.
Then picture her again in Genesis 21.
Weeping in the wilderness.
Unable to rescue her son.
Until God spoke.
Until her eyes were opened.
Until water was found.
The Bible does not tell us that Hagar's entire life became easy afterward.
It does not give us a beautiful ending to every question we might ask about her suffering.
But it tells us enough.
God saw her.
God heard.
God spoke.
God provided.
God remained faithful.
And the same Scriptures that preserve her story direct us toward the fullness of God's saving grace in Jesus Christ.
So when the enemy of your soul tempts you to believe that you are too insignificant to matter, remember Hagar.
When rejection makes you question your worth, remember Hagar.
When the wilderness seems endless, remember Hagar.
And when your heart needs more than reassurance, look to Jesus Christ.
Look to His cross.
Look to His empty tomb.
Look to the Savior who calls sinners to repentance, offers forgiveness by grace, and promises eternal life to all who believe in Him.
Your circumstances may not change overnight.
Your healing may take time.
Some relationships may never be restored.
Some losses will remain painful until the day Christ makes all things new.
But your suffering is not beyond His knowledge.
Your sin is not beyond His power to forgive when you turn to Him.
And your story is not beyond the redeeming purposes of His grace.
If you remember nothing else from Hagar's story, remember this:
The wilderness may be where people stopped looking for you, but it was never a place where God lost sight of you.
